# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Answer

| # | Standard | Level | Unit | Form (how the level is evaluated) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary **annual** PM2.5 | **9.0** | µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter) | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined per 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N |
| 2 | Primary **24-hour** PM2.5 | **35** | µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter) | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, determined per 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N |

Both are **primary** (health-based) standards. Units throughout are µg/m³, ambient concentration of PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter ≤ a nominal 2.5 micrometers).

## 2. Authority and verbatim regulatory text

**Citation:** 40 CFR § 50.20 — *National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5*, promulgated at **89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024)**; effective 60 days after publication (May 6, 2024).

> § 50.20 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.
>
> (a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are **9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration** and **35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration** measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:
>
> (1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or
>
> (2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.
>
> (b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is **less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3**.
>
> (c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is **less than or equal to 35 µg/m3**.
>
> [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]

Source retrieved: https://ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.20 (eCFR "current" text, fetched 2026-11-16); corroborated by the 2024 annual print of 40 CFR vol. 2 (GovInfo, same text and same source note).

## 3. Corroboration of the 2024 revision

EPA's PM NAAQS page states: "On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) ... EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter ... EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards, secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and primary and secondary PM10 standards."

EPA's designations page states the same in numeric form: "...strengthening the standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m3..."

Three independent renderings of the regulation (eCFR current, CFR annual print, EPA program pages) agree on 9.0 / 35.

## 4. Currency check — why 9.0 and not 12.0, and what would change the answer

- **12.0 µg/m³ is the superseded value.** It is the annual level of the prior § 50.18 standard (78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013). That section still appears in the 2024 CFR volume alongside the new § 50.20 and is a common source of stale citations. Do not report 12.0 as current.
- **35 µg/m³ has been stable since the 2006 review** and was expressly retained, unchanged, in both the 2012 and 2024 reviews. It is the low-risk half of this answer.
- **Open item to monitor, not a change in the codified standard:** EPA's PM NAAQS page carries a banner dated 03/12/2025, "Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5)." As of the eCFR snapshot used here (fetched 2026-11-16), § 50.20 still reads 9.0 / 35. An announcement or a proposed reconsideration does not amend the standard; only a final rule amending § 50.20 does. **Trigger to re-check:** any Federal Register final rule amending 40 CFR § 50.20, or any change to the eCFR "current" text of § 50.20. If the annual standard is revised, ask 1 changes; ask 2 changes only if the 24-hour standard is separately revised.
- **Designations are a separate matter.** EPA's initial designations for the 2024 revised annual standard were still in progress (notice of intended approach dated October 2, 2026). Designation status affects which areas are nonattainment; it does not change the 9.0 / 35 levels.

## 5. Scope notes and conventions

- **Primary only.** The request asks for primary standards. Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are out of scope here; do not substitute them. (EPA's 2024 notice states the secondary annual PM2.5 standard and the 24-hour PM2.5 standards, primary and secondary, were unchanged; the secondary annual level is not quoted in the source passages used here and is deliberately not restated.)
- **Units.** µg/m³ in all cases; no ppb/ppm conversion applies to PM2.5 mass concentrations. Do not convert or round to other units for reporting without labeling the conversion.
- **Rounding.** The regulation states levels to one decimal place for the annual standard (9.0) and as an integer for the 24-hour standard (35). Compliance is determined against the Appendix N data-handling and rounding conventions, not by informal rounding of the level itself; report the level exactly as codified ("9.0", not "9"; "35", not "35.0") to avoid implying spurious precision.
- **"Less than or equal to"** governs both standards: a value exactly at 9.0 µg/m³ (annual) or exactly at 35 µg/m³ (98th percentile 24-hour) is attainment.
- **Statistical form (context, not part of the numeric answer).** Appendix N specifies the multi-year averaging underlying both forms — the annual standard is evaluated on the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means, and the 24-hour standard on the 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour values. The three-year averaging detail is not quoted verbatim in the source passages above and should be confirmed against Appendix N before being relied on in a compliance calculation. The request asks only for levels, so the answer stands on § 50.20(a)–(c).
- **Federal vs. state/tribal.** These are the federal NAAQS. State or tribal implementation plans may impose more stringent requirements; that is outside this answer.

## 6. Re-verification procedure (to re-confirm before publication)

1. Open https://ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.20 and read paragraphs (a), (b), (c). Confirm the two bolded numbers and the source note "[89 FR ..., Mar. 6, 2024]" or later.
2. Confirm the section number is **§ 50.20**, not § 50.18 (the pre-2024 section still visible in older CFR volumes).
3. Cross-check against EPA's PM NAAQS page rule-history block for any final rule dated after Mar. 6, 2024 that amends the PM2.5 levels.
4. If any step yields a different annual or 24-hour number, report the newer codified number and cite its Federal Register page and effective date.

## 7. Common-error checklist

- 12.0 µg/m³ annual → **wrong**, superseded 2012 value.
- 15 µg/m³ annual → that is a *secondary* annual figure from earlier reviews, not the current primary standard; do not use for ask 1.
- 65 µg/m³ 24-hour → the pre-2006 24-hour level; long superseded.
- 35 µg/m³ annual → conflation of the 24-hour level with the annual level; wrong.
- 9 µg/m³ 24-hour → conflation in the other direction; wrong.

# General Industry Fall Protection Threshold — Unprotected Sides and Edges

## 1. Direct answer

**4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.**

Under the current federal OSHA general industry walking-working surfaces standard, the employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge when that surface is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level**.

**Citation:** 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i).

The rule states: 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:' guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

Because the rule says '4 feet (1.2 m) or more,' the duty attaches **at exactly 4 feet**, not only above 4 feet. Below 4 feet, the general side-and-edge rule in 1910.28(b)(1)(i) does not itself require fall protection, but other paragraphs of 1910.28 or other subparts may still apply.

## 2. How the threshold is applied

1. **Confirm the standard.** Use 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D for general industry. Do not apply the construction standard, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M, which generally triggers at 6 feet under 1926.501(b)(1).
2. **Identify the walking-working surface and the unprotected side or edge.** The hazard is an edge from which an employee could fall to a lower level.
3. **Measure the vertical distance** from the walking-working surface to the lower level at the edge. The measurement is the height above the lower level, not the height of a guardrail or the height of the employee.
4. **If the distance is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more,** provide one or more of the following: a guardrail system, a safety net system, or a personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system).
5. **Ensure the selected system meets the criteria in 29 CFR 1910.29.** For example, guardrail top rails must be 42 inches (107 cm) plus or minus 3 inches (8 cm) above the walking-working surface, with the other 1910.29 criteria met.
6. **Document the determination** — the surface, the edge, the measured height, the protection selected, and the inspection/maintenance record.

## 3. Important exceptions and separate triggers to check

The 4-foot rule is the general rule, but 1910.28 contains provisions that alter or add requirements. Check at least:

- **1910.28(a)(2) exemptions**, including portable ladders; pre-work/post-work inspections under the stated conditions; exposed perimeters of entertainment stages and rail-station platforms; powered platforms under 1910.66(j); aerial lifts under 1910.67(c)(2)(v); telecommunications work under 1910.268(n)(7) and (8); and electric power generation, transmission, and distribution work under 1910.269(g)(2)(i).
- **Dangerous equipment — 1910.28(b)(6).** An employee less than 4 feet above dangerous equipment must be protected from falling into or onto the equipment by a guardrail system or travel restraint system unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard; at 4 feet or more above dangerous equipment, the rule requires protection by guardrail systems and other listed means. This is a separate and sometimes stricter trigger.
- **Runways and similar walkways — 1910.28(b)(5).** The trigger is also 4 feet (1.2 m) or more to a lower level, with specific guardrail and feasibility provisions.
- **Fixed ladders — 1910.28(b)(9).** A different threshold applies to fixed ladders extending more than 24 feet (7.3 m) above a lower level for ladder safety systems, personal fall arrest systems, or other listed measures.
- **Low-slope roofs — 1910.28(b)(13).** The general 4-foot trigger applies, with a specific work-rule alternative (including a 15-foot distance from the roof edge) only where the employer can demonstrate that the specified systems are not feasible and the other conditions of that paragraph are met.
- **Pits, holes, and other specific surfaces** may have their own requirements under 1910.28(b).

## 4. Construction contrast — do not use 6 feet for this question

Construction work covered by 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) generally requires fall protection at **6 feet** above a lower level. That is not the general industry answer. For the general industry walking-working surface described in the request, the answer remains **4 feet (1.2 m) or more**.

## 5. Jurisdiction note

The answer above is the **federal OSHA** general industry requirement. A US state with an OSHA-approved state plan must have a standard at least as effective as the federal standard, but the state's adopted text may differ in detail or be stricter. For a workplace in a state-plan state, verify the state's current adopted standard; the federal threshold is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more.

## 6. Bottom line

**Protect at 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.** The employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge at that height by guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system, and must ensure the system meets 29 CFR 1910.29.

ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States under the general operating rules must carry fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, in addition, enough fuel to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. The reserve is 20 minutes. It is a time, not a fixed quantity of fuel; it becomes gallons/pounds by multiplying the aircraft's normal-cruise fuel consumption by one-third of an hour.

GOVERNING REGULATION — 14 CFR 91.151(b) (verbatim)

"(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Three operative elements:
1. The fuel is computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions (so the en-route leg is a wind-adjusted estimate, not still-air).
2. The 20 minutes is flown at normal cruising speed — the cruise power setting / TAS the flight is planned at, not max range speed, not max continuous power.
3. It is a minimum to BEGIN the flight; the rule prohibits dispatch below it, it does not authorize continuing once the reserve is eaten into.

DAY VERSUS NIGHT — NO DIFFERENCE FOR ROTORCRAFT

Unlike airplanes, the rotorcraft rule contains no day/night split. 91.151(a) gives airplanes 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night; 91.151(b) gives rotorcraft 20 minutes, full stop, day or night. A night VFR helicopter flight in the US under Part 91 still requires only the 20-minute reserve. Do not carry the airplane 30/45 numbers across.

SCOPE TABLE — WHICH RULE APPLIES

| Operation | Rule | VFR reserve beyond first point of intended landing |
|---|---|---|
| Helicopter, Part 91, VFR, day | 91.151(b) | 20 min at normal cruising speed |
| Helicopter, Part 91, VFR, night | 91.151(b) | 20 min at normal cruising speed (no night increase) |
| Helicopter, Part 135, VFR, day or night | 135.209(b) | 20 min (same figure; separate rule) |
| Helicopter, Part 91, IFR | 91.167(a) | 45 min at normal cruising speed after the first airport of intended landing (plus alternate fuel if an alternate is required) — not the VFR answer |
| Airplane, Part 91, VFR, day / night | 91.151(a) | 30 min / 45 min — not applicable to helicopters |

The 20-minute figure is therefore stable across Part 91 and Part 135 helicopter VFR operations; what changes with the operator is only any company-imposed margin on top.

CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A FUEL QUANTITY

Reserve (gal) = (20 / 60) x normal-cruise fuel burn (gal/hr) = 0.3333 x burn
Reserve (lb)  = (20 / 60) x normal-cruise fuel flow (lb/hr)

Worked examples (verify against the aircraft's own cruise figures, not these):
- Cruise burn 30 gal/hr -> 0.3333 x 30 = 10.0 gal reserve.
- Cruise burn 25 gal/hr -> 0.3333 x 25 = 8.3 gal reserve.
- Cruise burn 160 lb/hr -> 0.3333 x 160 = 53.3 lb reserve.

Note that the same 20 minutes is a smaller quantity at a low cruise burn and a larger one at a high burn; the regulation constrains time, not volume. The 20 minutes is also separate from, and additive to, unusable fuel, taxi/run-up fuel, and the fuel needed for the en-route leg itself.

WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS NOT

- It is not an alternate requirement. Part 91 VFR helicopter operations have no IFR-style alternate fuel requirement; the reserve is the whole of the regulatory pad.
- It is not a landing guarantee. Twenty minutes at cruise is roughly 20 minutes of range, not 20 minutes of hovering or 20 minutes of loiter; if the diversion needs a hover or a low-altitude search, the time available is shorter than the number suggests.
- It is not a planning target. It is the legal floor for beginning the flight. Standard practice and most training material treat it as a minimum to be exceeded when weather, terrain, or lack of en-route landing sites warrants; 91.103 already requires the pilot to become familiar with all available information, and known delays must be accounted for on top of the reserve.
- It is not affected by special VFR. SVFR changes weather minimums and clearance requirements, not the fuel reserve in 91.151(b).
- It is not reduced by carrying more fuel than required; carrying more is always permitted, carrying less is not.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR DISPATCH USE

Plan the en-route fuel to the first point of intended landing (wind-adjusted), then add 20 minutes of fuel at normal cruise power/fuel flow. That 20 minutes is the US legal VFR reserve for a helicopter, day or night, Part 91 or Part 135.

## Answer

**1. Deprecating RFC:** **RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (BCP 195, March 2021; IETF TLS Working Group; K. Moriarty and S. Farrell). It was published from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12.

**2. Status assigned to the defining RFCs:** **Historic**. RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were both moved to Historic status by RFC 8996. The same action moved RFC 4347 (DTLS 1.0) to Historic as well; RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) was also moved to Historic because the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic.

### Supporting text (RFC 8996 abstract, verbatim)

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996 Section 1 (Introduction) restates and widens the scope:

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

### Status summary table

| Document | Protocol version defined | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 2246 | TLS 1.0 | Historic |
| RFC 4346 | TLS 1.1 | Historic |
| RFC 4347 | DTLS 1.0 | Historic |
| RFC 5469 | DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS 1.0/1.1 | Historic |
| RFC 6347 | DTLS 1.2 | Updated (DTLS 1.0 negotiation now forbidden); not deprecated |
| RFC 5246 | TLS 1.2 | Not deprecated by this document (already superseded by RFC 8446) |
| RFC 7525 | BCP 195 TLS best practices | Updated |

### Terminology note (worth preserving in any write-up)

RFC 8996 performs two distinct IETF actions, and they should not be conflated:

- **Deprecating a protocol version** — the normative statement that TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0 must no longer be used.
- **Reclassifying documents** — the accompanying IESG/RFC Editor action moving RFC 2246, RFC 4346, RFC 4347 (and RFC 5469) to **Historic** stream status. The "Historic" label is the document status; "deprecated" is the protocol-version status. The question asks for the latter effect on the documents, and the answer is Historic.

RFC 8996 itself carries the status **Internet Best Current Practice** ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice") and is part of **BCP 195**, updating RFC 7525.

- RFC 8996 in the RFC Editor's inline-errata view: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc8996.html

answer:
US Social Security contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum) for calendar year 2026 = $184,500.

1. THE FIGURE

   Contribution and benefit base, 2026: $184,500

   This is the maximum amount of annual earnings subject to the Social Security (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance, OASDI) payroll tax in 2026. Earnings at or above this level are taxed on exactly $184,500; no OASDI tax is withheld or owed on earnings above it. The same $184,500 limit applies when those earnings are used in a benefit computation (i.e., it is simultaneously the contribution base and the benefit base).

2. SOURCES (all official, all fetched 2026-11-16, all in agreement)

   (a) SSA, Office of the Chief Actuary, 'Contribution and Benefit Base' — https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html
       The published series 'Contribution and benefit bases, 1937-2027' lists:
         2024  $168,600
         2025  $176,100
         2026  $184,500
         2027  $192,300
       The page's own definition, quoted: 'Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for a given year. The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used in a benefit computation. This limit changes each year with changes in the national average wage index. We call this annual limit the contribution and benefit base. This amount is also commonly referred to as the taxable maximum.'
       That the page is already publishing 2027 as its forward year establishes that the 2026 figure is final and officially determined, not a projection.

   (b) SSA, Detailed Calculator update page — https://www.ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html
       Quoted: 'The Social Security automatic cost-of-living adjustment for December 2025 and the wage-indexed amounts for 2026 were announced in the fall of 2025.' and, in the list of amounts required to update the calculator:
         'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500'
         '"Old-law" contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100'

   (c) IRS, Publication 926 (2026), Household Employer's Tax Guide — https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p926.pdf
       Quoted under 'What's New — Social security and Medicare taxes for 2026': 'The social security tax rate is 6.2% each for the employee and employer. The social security wage base limit is $184,500. The Medicare tax rate is 1.45% each for the employee and employer, unchanged from 2025. There is no wage base limit for Medicare tax.'

3. STATUTORY MECHANICS (why this number and not another)

   The base is set annually by the Social Security Administration under the automatic-adjustment provisions of the Social Security Act, indexed to the national average wage index (NAWI), with a statutory no-decrease provision. SSA announced the 2026 wage-indexed amounts in fall 2025 together with the December 2025 COLA of 2.8 percent and the 2024 NAWI of $69,846.57 (source (b)). Amounts for 1937–1974 and 1979–1981 were set by statute; all other years, including 2026, are automatic determinations.

4. COMPANION FIGURES (stated only where grounded; arithmetic shown in full)

   - OASDI tax rate on wages, 2026: 6.2% each for employee and employer (12.4% combined).
   - Maximum employee OASDI contribution, 2026: 184,500 x 0.062 = $11,439.00.
   - Maximum employer OASDI contribution per employee, 2026: 184,500 x 0.062 = $11,439.00.
   - Maximum self-employment (SECA) OASDI contribution, 2026: 184,500 x 0.124 = $22,878.00. The same $184,500 base applies to self-employment income under SECA.
   - Medicare (HI): NO earnings cap. The HI taxable maximum was aligned with the OASDI base only for 1966–1990 (last shared value $51,300); since 1991 there has been no limitation on HI-taxable earnings (source (a)). HI rates are 1.45% each for employee and employer and 2.90% for the self-employed. Do not apply $184,500 to Medicare withholding — it caps OASDI only.
   - 'Old-law' contribution and benefit base, 2026: $137,100 (source (b)). This is a separate technical figure used in certain benefit computations; it is not the payroll-tax base and must not be substituted for $184,500.

5. YEAR-OVER-YEAR CONTEXT

   2025: $176,100 -> 2026: $184,500. Increase = $8,400 = 4.77% (8,400 / 176,100 = 0.047699). The base rose, consistent with the no-decrease provision; no threshold or bound stated in this deliverable is violated by any figure above.

6. SCOPE AND CAVEATS

   - Jurisdiction: United States federal law (FICA for wages, SECA for self-employment). Not a state program and not another country's social security system.
   - The figure is the annual taxable maximum, not the tax rate, not the maximum benefit, and not the earnings required for a quarter of coverage. Earnings-per-quarter-of-coverage for 2026 is deliberately omitted: it was not present in the retrieved passages, and it is not required by the ask.
   - The figure is the officially announced value. No projection, estimate, or Trustees Report extrapolation is involved, and none should be substituted.
   - The base also governs the maximum Social Security retirement benefit computable for the 2026 cohort, but the dollar amount of that maximum benefit depends on age at claiming and is not stated here.

ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for tax year 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

AUTHORITY AND PROVENANCE

- Primary: IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments), which states that "[t]he limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500." This is the operative, officially announced 2026 figure — not a projection.
- Corroborating, independently: IRS Publication 560 (2025 tax-year edition, "What's New"): "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026. These limits apply for participants in SARSEPs, 401(k) plans (excluding SIMPLE plans), section 403(b) plans, and section 457(b) plans."
- Corroborating: IRS Retirement Topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."
- Corroborating (403(b) analogue, same dollar figure): IRS Publication 571 (1-2026): "the most that can be contributed to your 403(b) account through a salary reduction agreement is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026."

WHAT THE FIGURE DOES AND DOES NOT INCLUDE

- Included: pre-tax elective deferrals and Roth elective deferrals made under a §401(k) cash-or-deferred arrangement. The $24,500 is a single combined cap — Roth and pre-tax deferrals share it; electing Roth does not create additional room.
- Excluded (by the terms of the question): catch-up contributions under §414(v). For 2026 those are $8,000 for participants age 50 or older, and $11,250 for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026. Adding these to the base limit gives totals of $32,500 and $35,750 respectively — those totals are NOT the answer to this question and are given only to show the arithmetic boundary.
- Excluded: employer matching and nonelective contributions, which sit under the §415(c) annual additions limit of $72,000 for 2026, not under §402(g).
- Excluded: after-tax (non-Roth) employee contributions, which are not elective deferrals.

QUALIFIERS AN HR/PAYROLL PRACTITIONER MUST APPLY

1. 100%-of-compensation cap. §402(g)(1) limits the exclusion to the lesser of the dollar limit or 100% of the employee's compensation. $24,500 is the ceiling for a normally-paid employee; a very low-paid employee's effective cap is their compensation.
2. Plan-specific limits may bind lower. The $24,500 is a statutory maximum, not an entitlement. The plan document may set a lower cap, and ADP nondiscrimination testing under §401(k)(3) can reduce a highly compensated employee's permitted deferrals below $24,500 (excess amounts above the ADP-permitted level are refunded to the HCE). Safe harbor and QACA designs avoid ADP, but a QACA's default-escalation schedule still operates within the same $24,500 statutory cap.
3. Aggregation across plans. The $24,500 is an individual limit across all 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, and governmental 457(b) deferrals the employee makes with all employers in the year (403(b) contracts of one employer are aggregated; the 15-year rule under §402(g)(7) for 403(b) is a separate, narrow exception). An employee with two jobs does not get $24,500 per job.
4. §401(a)(17) compensation limit for 2026 is $360,000; it constrains the compensation base used in ADP testing and §415(c), not the $24,500 itself.
5. Not the SIMPLE limit. SIMPLE 401(k)/SIMPLE IRA deferrals for 2026 are $17,000. If the employee is in a SIMPLE plan, $24,500 is the wrong number.
6. Not the starter-401(k) limit. Deferral-only starter 401(k)/safe harbor 403(b)(16) arrangements remain at $6,000 for 2026 (plus $1,100 at age 50+).

OPERATIONAL PROCEDURE (payroll / plan administration)

Step 1. Set the per-employee deferral election cap at $24,500 for calendar year 2026 (or the plan year, if the plan uses a non-calendar limitation year — confirm the plan's §402(g) limitation year; absent contrary plan terms it is the calendar year).
Step 2. Configure the payroll system to test cumulative YTD §402(g) deferrals (pre-tax + Roth) against $24,500 and to hard-stop or suspend deferrals on the pay date the cap is reached. Do not net employer match against this test.
Step 3. Track catch-up eligibility separately: only after the $24,500 (or the ADP/plan limit, if lower) is reached may amounts be coded as catch-up, and only up to $8,000 (or $11,250 for ages 60–63 in 2026).
Step 4. At year-end, run a §402(g) excess-deferral test across all plans and prior employers disclosed by the employee. Excess deferrals plus attributable earnings must be distributed by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation; the excess is includible in gross income in the year deferred.
Step 5. If the employee is an HCE, run the ADP test before treating $24,500 as the operative cap for that individual, and process corrective distributions within 2½ months after the plan year end (12 months to avoid the employer excise tax under §4979).

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE REQUESTER

2026 §402(g) elective deferral limit for a 401(k): $24,500 (USD), before catch-up. This is the announced, final figure per IRS Notice 2025-67, not an inflation estimate. It may be reduced for a specific employee by the 100%-of-compensation cap, the plan document, or ADP testing, and it must be aggregated across all of that employee's 401(k)/403(b)/SARSEP/governmental 457(b) deferrals.

BasicMed aircraft limits — current US law (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as amended by PL 118-63 § 828, effective 12 November 2024)

ANSWERS

| Limit | Current value | Regulatory character |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum takeoff weight | 12,500 lb (maximum certificated takeoff weight) | Aircraft attribute, set by the design approval |
| Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 occupants, including the pilot and any other required flightcrew | Aircraft attribute, set by the design approval |
| Passengers on board | 6 passengers | Operating limitation on the flight |

How the three fit together (this is the part people get wrong): 'occupants' is a property of the aircraft — what its type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended type certificate authorizes it to carry. 'Passengers' is a property of the flight — how many non-flightcrew persons are actually aboard. Because the pilot in command is an occupant but not a passenger, the two caps are consistent: 6 passengers + 1 PIC = 7 occupants, exactly at the authorization ceiling. In an aircraft certificated for two required pilots, 7 occupants − 2 flightcrew = 5 passengers, so the occupant cap binds before the passenger cap does. Whichever cap is reached first governs.

CURRENCY — READ THIS BEFORE CITING ANY OTHER SOURCE

The figures above are the post-November 2024 figures. Guidance still in wide circulation states the pre-2024 numbers, and those are now wrong:

| Source | MTOW | Occupants | Passengers | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FAA newsroom, 'FAA Updates BasicMed Program,' 15 Nov 2024 | 12,500 lb (from 6,000) | 7 (from 6) | 6 (from 5) | Current |
| FAA Order/Notice N 8000.386, 14 Nov 2024, ¶5.a(2) | 12,500 lb | 7 | 6 — 'will apply on or after November 12, 2024' | Current |
| FAA BasicMed airmen page (as fetched) | 'not more than 12,500 pounds' | 'not more than 7 occupants' | 'not more than six passengers' | Current |
| AC 68-1A, 3 May 2017, ¶¶3.2, 5.2.1 | 6,000 lb | 6 | 5 | SUPERSEDED |
| FAA Safety Briefing, Jul/Aug 2017, 'Know Your BasicMed Operating Limits' | 6,000 lb | 6 | 5 | SUPERSEDED |

If a client, insurer, FBO, or rental checkout sheet hands you 6,000 lb / 6 / 5, that document predates 12 November 2024. The 2017 AC is the single most common source of the stale figures because it is still the numbered advisory circular of record for BasicMed and has not been reissued at the time of writing — treat the AC's Part 5 numbers as historical and the FAA notice/newsroom figures as operative.

REGULATORY BASIS

- Operative limits: 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), amended per PL 118-63 (FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024) § 828, 'Expansion of BasicMed,' effective 12 November 2024.
- Part 68 (14 CFR part 68) is the eligibility and examination procedure — checklist (CMEC, FAA Form 8700-2), state-licensed physician exam, medical education course, driver's license, and the prohibition on acting as PIC during medical deficiency. Part 68 does not itself contain the aircraft limits; do not cite it for the three numbers.
- For determining what a specific aircraft is 'authorized to carry,' the design approval controls (TC, STC, or ATC) — see AC 68-1A ¶5.1.2, whose reasoning survives the 2024 amendment even though its numbers do not. Seat count installed is not the test; a variant certificated for more occupants than it has seats does not qualify.

RELATED LIMITS (not asked, stated only so the three numbers are not mistaken for the whole rule)

- Operation within the United States (or another country in which BasicMed is authorized), at or below 18,000 ft MSL, at an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots.
- No operation for compensation or hire.
- VFR or IFR; day or night.
- Pilot must act as PIC; may not serve as safety pilot unless also acting as PIC.
- The operational limitations apply to the entire flight, takeoff to touchdown — if the flight exceeds them at any point, a BasicMed pilot may not act as PIC at any point on that flight, even while another pilot with a medical certificate is at the controls.
- The 12,500 lb increase excludes transport-category helicopters (FAA newsroom, 15 Nov 2024); those remain subject to the lower weight limit.

CAVEAT NOT RESOLVED BY THE AVAILABLE TEXT

The experimental-aircraft occupant route is addressed through 14 CFR 91.319(j). AC 68-1A described that section as prohibiting operation of an experimental aircraft under BasicMed with more than six occupants. Whether § 91.319(j) was conformed to seven occupants by the 2024 expansion is not established by the sources retrieved for this answer. For a type-certificated aircraft the table above is complete and reliable; for an experimental aircraft, verify § 91.319(j) current text before relying on the 7-occupant figure.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR A FLIGHT-PLANNING NOTE

Under BasicMed (current, post-12 Nov 2024): aircraft authorized to carry no more than 7 occupants, maximum certificated takeoff weight no more than 12,500 lb, and no more than 6 passengers on board.
